2 PyTorch in ten lines

Tensors. A tensor is a block of numbers with a shape. A batch of images has four axes, (N, C, H, W). Most errors are shape errors: print .shape.

A model is a function with parameters. nn.Module classes create layers in __init__ and say how data flows in forward. You call model(x), never model.forward(x). This is the MLP of the warm-up:

# S2·W4 (extract)
class MLP(nn.Module):
    """flatten → Linear(3072, 64) → ReLU → Linear(64, 10)."""
    def __init__(self, in_features=3 * 32 * 32, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(),                     # (N, 3, 32, 32) -> (N, 3072)
                                 nn.Linear(in_features, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.Linear(hidden, 10))            # (N, 10) logits

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)                                # logits, no softmax

Logits and probabilities. The model’s 10 outputs are logits: raw scores. Softmax turns them into probabilities (between 0 and 1, adding to 1). nn.CrossEntropyLoss wants the logits: it already contains a softmax inside (safer numerically). A second softmax in forward would be applied twice and hurt training. So the notebook applies softmax only to show probabilities, and every forward ends with logits, no softmax.

The four steps of training, repeated for every batch of every epoch. This is the heart of fit (in S2·0):

# S2·0 (extract)
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        perm = torch.randperm(n, device=X_train.device)          # a new random order every epoch
        total = torch.zeros((), device=X_train.device)          # sum of the losses of this epoch
        for i in range(0, n, batch_size):
            idx = perm[i:i + batch_size]                          # the indices of one mini-batch
            xb, yb = X_train[idx], y_train[idx]
            loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)        # 1. forward, 2. loss
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()                      # 3. backward (gradients)
            optimizer.step()                     # 4. update the parameters

model.train() and model.eval() switch layers such as BatchNorm between training and testing behaviour. torch.no_grad() stops PyTorch from recording gradients: use it when you do not call backward() (the decorator @torch.no_grad() does it for a whole function). argmax(dim=1) gives, for each row, the position of the largest score: the predicted class.

# S2·0 (extract)
@torch.no_grad()                         # no gradients needed to predict: faster, less memory
def predict(model, X, batch_size=1000):
    """Predicted class of every image in X, computed in batches of 1,000 so the GPU memory is enough."""
    model.eval()
    preds = []
    for i in range(0, len(X), batch_size):
        logits = model(X[i:i + batch_size])          # (batch, 10): one score per class
        preds.append(logits.argmax(dim=1))          # (batch,): the class with the largest score
    return torch.cat(preds)

3 Part 0 · Setup (S2·0)

What it does. It prepares everything (about 20 s on a T4 the first time). It has about 340 lines, but only four ideas matter: it finds the GPU (device), defines helpers (check, count_params, fit, predict, evaluate, show_grid, report_line), loads CIFAR-10 and loads ResNet18 pretrained on ImageNet with four test photos. In: nothing. Out: CIFAR_X_TRAIN (50000, 3, 32, 32) of integers 0 to 255, CIFAR_Y_TRAIN (50000,), the model resnet, PHOTOS_224 (four tensors (1, 3, 224, 224)), and categories (1,000 class names). The notebook says it too: “You do not need to read this cell”. These are the fragments that matter.

1. Loading CIFAR-10. It tries three sources (disk, a mirror on Hugging Face, the original site). This turns the images into a tensor:

# S2·0 (extract)
        CIFAR_X_TRAIN = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(tr_np)).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).contiguous()
        CIFAR_X_TEST = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(te_np)).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).contiguous()
Code What it means
np.asarray(tr_np) The images as an array (N, 32, 32, 3): height, width, colour (the order of image files).
.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) Reorder the axes to (N, C, H, W): PyTorch wants the channels before the pixels.

2. Loading ResNet18 and its normalization constants.

# S2·0 (extract)
weights = ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT
categories = weights.meta["categories"]                  # a list of 1,000 names, e.g. categories[0] = "tench"
resnet = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights=weights).eval().to(device)
IMAGENET_MEAN = torch.tensor([0.485, 0.456, 0.406]).view(1, 3, 1, 1)     # one mean per colour channel
IMAGENET_STD = torch.tensor([0.229, 0.224, 0.225]).view(1, 3, 1, 1)      # one std per colour channel
Code What it means
weights.meta["categories"] The names of the 1,000 classes (“tabby”, “espresso”, …).
.to(device) Move all parameters to the GPU. Data must be on the same device, or PyTorch complains.
.view(1, 3, 1, 1) Reshape the 3 numbers to (1, 3, 1, 1) so they can be broadcast against (N, 3, H, W): each colour gets its own number.

3. imagenet_norm and center_224. ResNet18 was trained on photos normalized per colour (subtract the ImageNet mean, divide by its standard deviation) and of size 224 × 224. We must do the same.

# S2·0 (extract)
def imagenet_norm(x):
    """Pixels in [0, 1] -> the normalization ResNet18 was trained with (ImageNet mean and std per channel)."""
    return (x - IMAGENET_MEAN.to(x.device)) / IMAGENET_STD.to(x.device)
# ...
def center_224(x, size=224):
    """Resize the short side to 224 and cut the central 224 × 224 square (what ResNet18 expects)."""
    h, w = x.shape[-2:]
    s = size / min(h, w)                                  # scale factor for the short side
    new_h, new_w = max(size, round(h * s)), max(size, round(w * s))
    x = F.interpolate(x, size=(new_h, new_w), mode="bilinear", antialias=True, align_corners=False)
    top, left = (new_h - size) // 2, (new_w - size) // 2  # where the central square starts
    return x[..., top:top + size, left:left + size].clamp(0, 1)
Code What it means
F.interpolate(x, size=..., mode="bilinear") Resize by smooth averaging. antialias=True avoids jagged edges when shrinking.
x[..., top:top + size, left:left + size] Cut a square. The three dots mean “all the leading axes” (N and C).

Expect: device: cuda, CIFAR-10 from the Hugging Face mirror, a download bar (45 MB), the photo sizes, ResNet18: 11,689,512 parameters, 1000 classes, setup ready in ... s (about 15 s on the reference run). If you see: device: cpu (change the runtime); CIFAR-10 from ... failed (it tries the next source, wait a minute); using Fashion-MNIST instead (all sources failed, clothes instead of CIFAR-10: tell the lecturer); NameError: name 'resnet' is not defined in a later cell (S2·0 did not finish or the runtime restarted: run it again).

What it does. out_size gives the side of the output of a convolution or a pooling. In: J (input size), M (kernel), P (padding), S (stride). Out: one whole number.

# ✏️ S2·W1
def out_size(J, M, P=0, S=1):
    """Output size of a convolution or pooling: input J, kernel M, padding P, stride S."""
    # TODO: add the padding on both sides, remove the kernel, divide by the stride (integer division)

# four examples: expected 28, 28, 112, 14
print(out_size(28, 3, 1), out_size(32, 5), out_size(224, 7, 3, 2), out_size(28, 2, 0, 2))

P=0, S=1 are default values (used if you leave them out: out_size(32, 5)). // is integer division: it divides and rounds down, the “rounded down” of the formula.

Hint ✏. The formula is in the markdown above the cell and uses the same letters as the function line. Write it on paper first. In 2 * ___, which quantity is added on both sides of the image? Expect: four numbers; the ✅ cell checks four cases, including the first layers of LeNet and ResNet18.

# ✏️ S2·W2
def conv_params(M, C_in, C_out):
    """Weights and biases of nn.Conv2d(C_in, C_out, M)."""
    # TODO: weights of ONE filter (it sees every input channel) plus 1 bias, times the number of filters
    return (M * M * ___ + 1) * ___


# three examples: expected 80, 1168, 224
print(conv_params(3, 1, 8), conv_params(3, 8, 16), conv_params(3, 3, 8))

Hint ✏. One filter looks at an M × M patch of every input channel: how many weights? Add its single bias. Then, how many filters does the layer have? Expect: three numbers; the ✅ cell compares the third with PyTorch’s own nn.Conv2d.

4.3 W3 · write the CIFAR-10 ConvNet (S2·W3)

What it does. You complete an nn.Module for colour photos. In: (N, 3, 32, 32). Out: (N, 10) logits. The cell sends 64 random images through it to test the shapes.

# ✏️ S2·W3
class ConvNet(nn.Module):
    """conv(3→8) → ReLU → pool → conv(8→16) → ReLU → pool → flatten → Linear(1024, 64) → ReLU → Linear(64, 10)
    (the table above, as PyTorch layers)."""
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # TODO: colour photos have how many input channels? Which padding keeps 32 × 32 with a 3 × 3 kernel?
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(___, 8, kernel_size=3, padding=___)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(8, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.pool = nn.MaxPool2d(2)                        # halves height and width, 0 parameters
        # TODO: 16 channels times (height × width) after two poolings of a 32 × 32 photo
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(16 * ___, 64)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(64, 10)

    def forward(self, x):                          # x: (N, 3, 32, 32)
        x = F.relu(self.conv1(x))                  # (N, 8, 32, 32)
        x = self.pool(x)                           # (N, 8, 16, 16)
        x = F.relu(self.conv2(x))                  # (N, 16, 16, 16)
        x = self.pool(x)                           # (N, 16, 8, 8)
        x = x.flatten(1)                           # (N, 1024): one long vector per photo
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))                    # (N, 64)
        return self.fc2(x)                         # (N, 10) logits, no softmax


set_seed(0)
cnn_w = ConvNet()
out = cnn_w(torch.randn(64, 3, 32, 32))            # a batch of 64 random "photos", only to test the shapes
print("output", tuple(out.shape), "·", f"{count_params(cnn_w):,}", "parameters")
Code What it means
nn.Conv2d(in, out, kernel_size=3, padding=...) 3 × 3 filters. padding adds a frame of zeros, so the image can keep its size.
x.flatten(1) A list of numbers per image: keep axis 0 (the batch), merge all the others. (N, 16, H, W) becomes (N, 16·H·W).
nn.Linear(n_in, 64) n_in must equal the length of the list you give it.

Hints ✏ (three blanks). Input channels: how many values per pixel has a colour photo? Which axis of (N, C, H, W) is that? padding: the output side must equal the input side; use your W1 formula with M = 3, S = 1 and try P = 0, 1, 2 on paper. Linear input: follow Figure 3 and the shape comments in forward: each pooling halves height and width; the blank is the part after 16 *.

If you see: RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (64xA and Bx64): A is what flatten(1) really gives, B is what you wrote; recompute 16 × H × W. TypeError: not all arguments converted during string formatting inside Conv2d: the channels blank is still ___. NameError: name 'out' is not defined in the ✅ cell: the cell above failed. Expect: output (64, 10) · ... parameters; the ✅ cell tells you if both are right.

4.4 W4 · MLP against your ConvNet (S2·W4)

What it does. Trains the MLP and your ConvNet for 5 epochs on CIFAR-10 and draws two bars (about 10 s on a T4). In: your ConvNet (W3 must be right). Out: two accuracies and the REPORT line.

# S2·W4 (extract)
N_W, NV_W, EPOCHS_W = (10_000, 2_000, 1) if FAST else (50_000, 10_000, 5)

# the data: integers 0 to 255 -> floats in [0, 1] -> mean 0 and std 1 per colour channel
xw = CIFAR_X_TRAIN[:N_W].float() / 255                       # (50000, 3, 32, 32)
W_MEAN = xw.mean(dim=(0, 2, 3), keepdim=True)                # (1, 3, 1, 1): one mean per channel
W_STD = xw.std(dim=(0, 2, 3), keepdim=True)                  # (1, 3, 1, 1): one std per channel
Xw_train = ((xw - W_MEAN) / W_STD).to(device)
xw_val = CIFAR_X_TEST[:NV_W].float() / 255                   # (10000, 3, 32, 32)
Xw_val = ((xw_val - W_MEAN) / W_STD).to(device)              # same mean and std as the training photos
yw_train = CIFAR_Y_TRAIN[:N_W].to(device)
yw_val = CIFAR_Y_TEST[:NV_W].to(device)
del xw, xw_val
# ...
mlp_w, cnn_w = MLP(), ConvNet()
check(count_params(mlp_w) == 197322 and count_params(cnn_w) == 67642,
      "MLP 197,322 and ConvNet 67,642 parameters", "finish W3 first: the ConvNet must have 67,642 parameters")
fit(mlp_w, Xw_train, yw_train, Xw_val, yw_val, epochs=EPOCHS_W, name="MLP · CIFAR-10")
fit(cnn_w, Xw_train, yw_train, Xw_val, yw_val, epochs=EPOCHS_W, name="ConvNet · CIFAR-10")
Code What it means
.mean(dim=(0, 2, 3), keepdim=True) One average per colour channel: average over images, rows, columns; keepdim=True keeps the shape (1, 3, 1, 1) ready to subtract.
(xw - W_MEAN) / W_STD Normalization: each channel gets mean 0 and spread 1; training is faster and more stable.

Predict first, then run. Expect: one line per epoch, a bar chart, ✅ lines and REPORT: CIFAR-10 accuracy in % · MLP ... · CNN .... The reference Colab run gave about 49% for the MLP and 62% for the ConvNet: a few points of difference is fine, and the ConvNet must win with one third of the parameters. If you see: NameError: name 'ConvNet' is not defined (run W3 and its ✅ cell first); ❌ ... the ConvNet must have 67,642 parameters (W3 is wrong or was not rerun).

5 Lab 1 · Look inside VGG-16 and ResNet18

5.1 L1·1 · ResNet18 names four photos (S2·L1·1)

What it does. Gives four photos to the pretrained ResNet18 and prints its three best guesses. In: a photo (1, 3, 224, 224). Out: three (name, probability) pairs.

# ▶ S2·L1·1
@torch.no_grad()                                 # no gradients needed: we only look at the answer
def top_k(x, k=3):
    """The k most likely ImageNet classes of image x (pixels in [0, 1]) as a list of (name, probability)."""
    resnet.eval()
    logits = resnet(imagenet_norm(x))            # (1, 1000): one score per ImageNet class
    probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=1)[0]          # (1000,) probabilities: softmax here, never in the model
    vals, idx = probs.topk(k)                    # the k largest probabilities and their class numbers
    top = []
    for v, i in zip(vals, idx):
        top.append((categories[i], v.item()))
    return top


# plotting only: you can skip the imshow and title lines
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 3.6))
for a, (name, x) in zip(ax, PHOTOS_224.items()):
    top = top_k(x)
    REF["lab1"]["top1"][name] = top[0][0]
    print(f"{name:10s} " + " · ".join(f"{c} {100 * p:.1f}%" for c, p in top))
    a.imshow(x[0].permute(1, 2, 0).cpu()); a.axis("off")
    a.set_title(f"{top[0][0]} ({100 * top[0][1]:.0f}%)", fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# a low top-1 probability is a warning: maybe the photo shows none of the 1,000 classes
for name, x in PHOTOS_224.items():
    c, p = top_k(x, 1)[0]
    if p < 0.5:
        print(f"warning: '{name}' -> {c} at only {100 * p:.0f}%: the network is not sure "
              f"(is '{name}' one of its classes?)")
check(len(categories) == 1000, "ResNet18 chooses among 1,000 ImageNet classes", "rerun S2·0")
Code What it means
F.softmax(logits, dim=1)[0] Logits to probabilities along the class axis; [0] takes the only image of the batch: 1,000 numbers.
probs.topk(k) The k largest values and their positions.
x[0].permute(1, 2, 0).cpu() To draw with imshow: image 0, axes (C, H, W) to (H, W, C), moved to the CPU.

Expect: the cat and the coffee get sensible answers (the coffee about 93%). The astronaut and the rocket get wrong answers with low confidence: they are not among the 1,000 classes, so the network must pick the closest one. A classifier always answers; a low confidence is the warning.

The bias count is the number of outputs of this layer (the markdown states the sizes, and fc2 just below shows a complete line). What it does. Prints the end of ResNet18 and counts its FC layer. In: resnet from S2·0. Out: a count and a share.

# ✏️ S2·L1·TODO2

Hint ✏. Every layer of a model is an attribute with a name: resnet.conv1, resnet.layer1, … The name you need is in the markdown; write it without quotes. The head is tiny because the layer before it, avgpool, squeezes each 7 × 7 map to one number. 5.4 TODO 3 · a residual block (S2·L1·TODO3)

A plain block computes y = ReLU(F(x)). A residual block adds its input back: y = ReLU(x + F(x)).

# ✏️ S2·L1·TODO3
class Block(nn.Module):
    """F(x) = Linear → ReLU → Linear. With skip: y = ReLU(x + F(x)). Without: y = ReLU(F(x))."""
    def __init__(self, width, skip=True):
        super().__init__()
        self.f = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(width, width), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(width, width))   # F(x)
        self.skip = skip                         # True: residual block, False: plain block

    def forward(self, x):                        # x: (batch, width); the output has the same shape
        if self.skip:
            # TODO: y = x + F(x): what do we add back to F(x)?
            return F.relu(___ + self.f(x))       # residual block: add the input back
        return F.relu(self.f(x))                 # plain block

Hint ✏. In Figure 4, what travels along the extra path? Its name is in the line def forward(self, x). The ✅ cell sets all weights to 0, so F(x) = 0 (“learned nothing”): the residual block then returns its input, the plain block returns zeros. A block that learns nothing is harmless: that is ResNet’s idea. If you see: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "Tensor") to str (in the ✅ cell or in L1·3): the blank in the return line is still ___.

5.5 L1·3 · the gradient with and without skips (S2·L1·3)

What it does. Stacks 5 blocks (plain, then residual), runs one batch and measures the gradient at the first layer; then repeats for 1 to 30 blocks and plots it (log scale). CPU, fixed seed: everybody gets the same numbers. In: your Block. Out: two numbers, their ratio, a plot, the REPORT line.

# S2·L1·3 (extract)
def first_layer_grad(depth, skip, seed=0, width=WIDTH):
    """Mean |gradient| of the weights of the FIRST Linear layer, at initialization, on one random batch."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)                             # same seed -> same initial weights
    layers = []
    for _ in range(depth):
        layers.append(Block(width, skip))               # depth blocks, all plain or all residual
    layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 10))                 # output layer: 10 class scores
    net = nn.Sequential(*layers)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1000 + seed)
    x = torch.randn(64, width, generator=g)             # a random batch of 64 inputs: (64, 128)
    y = torch.randint(0, 10, (64,), generator=g)        # random labels: (64,)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(net(x), y)
    loss.backward()                                     # fills .grad of every weight
    first_weights = net[0].f[0].weight                  # the weights of the first Linear of the first block
    return first_weights.grad.abs().mean().item()       # their mean |gradient|
# ...
grad_plain = first_layer_grad(DEPTH, skip=False)
grad_skip = first_layer_grad(DEPTH, skip=True)
grad_ratio = grad_skip / grad_plain
Code What it means
nn.Sequential(*layers) The * unpacks the list into separate arguments: a chain of blocks plus an output layer.
net[0].f[0].weight The weights of the first layer (block 0, its function f, layer 0). Its .grad exists only after backward().

Expect: the gradient without skips is about a thousand times smaller (the ✅ line prints your ratio), the plot’s two lines drift apart, then REPORT: % of parameters in FC layers · VGG-16 ... · ResNet18 ... · gradient ratio skip/plain .... Without skips the first layer gets a tiny signal and learns very slowly; with skips the gradient has a direct path back. The ★ cell prints the ratio for 2 to 30 blocks.

6 Lab 2 · Grad-CAM, then fool the network

6.1 L2·1 · filters and feature maps (S2·L2·1)

What it does. Draws the 64 filters of the first layer, then keeps the outputs of two inner layers with forward hooks and draws 8 maps of each. In: the cat photo. Out: layer1 (1, 64, 56, 56) and layer4 (1, 512, 7, 7).

# S2·L2·1 (extract)
w1 = resnet.conv1.weight.detach().cpu()                     # (64, 3, 7, 7): 64 filters, 3 colours, 7 × 7
print("conv1 weights:", tuple(w1.shape))
show_grid(w1, ncols=16, size=0.75)                          # each filter scaled to [0, 1] as an RGB tile
# ...
maps = {}                                                   # the hooks put the layer outputs here


def save_output(name):
    """A forward hook: keeps the output of a layer in maps[name]."""
    def hook(module, inp, out):
        maps[name] = out.detach()
    return hook


hook1 = resnet.layer1.register_forward_hook(save_output("layer1"))
hook4 = resnet.layer4.register_forward_hook(save_output("layer4"))
with torch.no_grad():
    resnet(imagenet_norm(PHOTOS_224["cat"]))                # one forward pass: the hooks fill maps
hook1.remove()                                              # always remove hooks you do not need any more
hook4.remove()

A hook is a function that PyTorch calls for you while data goes through a layer. A forward hook receives (module, input, output). It is the way to read an inner layer without changing the network.

Code What it means
.detach().cpu() .detach(): cut the tensor from the gradient machinery; .cpu(): bring it to the CPU, which plotting needs.
def save_output(name): ... def hook(...) A function that returns a function: the inner hook remembers name.
layer1.register_forward_hook(f) “Whenever layer1 runs, call f too.” Returns a handle.
hook4.remove() Always remove hooks you no longer need, or they run in every later forward pass.

Expect: first-layer filters like edges at several angles and colour blobs; layer1 maps still look like the cat (56 × 56); layer4 maps are tiny (7 × 7).

6.2 TODO 1 · Grad-CAM (S2·L2·TODO1)

The idea. Which part of the photo made the network say “espresso”? layer4 has 512 maps of 7 × 7. Weight each map by how much it matters for the class score (the average gradient of the score with respect to that map), add them, and look at the 7 × 7 result as a heat map.

# ✏️ S2·L2·TODO1
def grad_cam(x, class_idx=None):
    """Grad-CAM map (1, 7, 7) of image x (pixels in [0, 1]) for one class (None = the top-1 class)."""
    store = {}                                   # the two hooks put acts and grads here

    def save_grad(g):                            # gradient hook: d(score) / d(acts), called by backward()
        store["grads"] = g

    def save_acts(module, inp, out):             # forward hook on layer4, called by the forward pass
        store["acts"] = out                      # (1, 512, 7, 7): 512 maps of 7 × 7
        out.register_hook(save_grad)             # ask for the gradient of these maps too

    handle = resnet.layer4.register_forward_hook(save_acts)
    try:
        logits = resnet(imagenet_norm(x))        # (1, 1000): one score per class
        if class_idx is None:
            class_idx = logits.argmax(dim=1).item()
        logits[0, class_idx].backward()          # gradient of ONE class score
    finally:
        handle.remove()                          # remove the hook, even if something failed
        resnet.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)       # forget the gradients of the weights (we do not train)
    acts = store["acts"].detach()                # (1, 512, 7, 7)
    grads = store["grads"]                       # (1, 512, 7, 7)
    # TODO: average over the 7 × 7 positions: which two dimensions of (1, 512, 7, 7) are height and width?
    w = grads.mean(dim=(___, ___), keepdim=True)               # (1, 512, 1, 1): one weight per map
    # TODO: add up the 512 weighted maps: which dimension counts the maps?
    cam = F.relu((w * acts).sum(dim=___))                      # (1, 7, 7): weighted sum of the 512 maps
    return cam, class_idx


# None = the top-1 class (espresso). Try another one, e.g. CLASS = categories.index("cup")
CLASS = None
cam, cam_cls = grad_cam(PHOTOS_224["coffee"], CLASS)
print("class:", categories[cam_cls], "· map", tuple(cam.shape))
cam_scaled = cam[0] / cam.max()                  # (7, 7) scaled so that the largest value is 1
print(cam_scaled.cpu().numpy().round(2))
Code What it means
out.register_hook(save_grad) Attach a gradient hook to the tensor out: backward() calls it with the gradient of out.
logits[0, class_idx].backward() Backward from one class score (not the loss): the gradients say what raises that class.
try: ... finally: The finally part always runs: the hook is removed even after an error.
grads.mean(dim=(___, ___), keepdim=True) Average over two axes: one weight per map, shape (1, 512, 1, 1).
(w * acts).sum(dim=___) Weight each map, then add the 512 maps into one: (1, 7, 7). F.relu keeps what raises the score.

Hints ✏ (three blanks). acts and grads have shape (1, 512, 7, 7). Count axes from 0: which two are the 7 × 7 positions? Those are averaged. The sum adds the 512 maps: along which axis do they live? Expect: class: espresso and a 7 × 7 grid of numbers from 0 to 1 (the largest is the hottest cell). The ✅ cell draws an overlay and prints the hottest cell, the REPORT of this lab. Two lines of it are worth reading:

# S2·L2·TODO1·check (extract)
flat_index = cam[0].argmax().item()             # position of the largest value among the 49 cells (0 to 48)
hot_cell = divmod(flat_index, 7)                # -> (row, col) in the 7 × 7 grid
# ...
heat = F.interpolate(cam[None], size=224, mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)[0, 0].cpu()

flat_index counts the 49 cells from 0 to 48, row by row; divmod(a, 7) gives the quotient and remainder: the row and the column. F.interpolate(cam[None], size=224, ...) stretches the 7 × 7 map to 224 × 224 for the overlay (cam[None] adds the batch axis it needs). Look at the overlay: is the heat where you expected? If you see: TypeError: mean(): argument 'dim' must be tuple of ints, not tuple and then NameError: name 'cam' is not defined: the blanks of the mean are still ___.

6.3 TODO 2 · fool the network with FGSM (S2·L2·TODO2)

The idea. The fast gradient sign method moves every pixel by a tiny ε in the direction that increases the loss: take the gradient of the loss with respect to the pixels (not the weights), keep its direction, scale by ε, add, and stay inside [0, 1].

# ✏️ S2·L2·TODO2
class Normalized(nn.Module):
    """Pixels in [0, 1] in, logits out: the ImageNet normalization is inside the model."""
    def __init__(self, model):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model

    def forward(self, x):                            # x: pixels in [0, 1]
        return self.model(imagenet_norm(x))


net = Normalized(resnet).eval()
EPS = [0.001, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1]   # 0.001 = 0.1% of the pixel range
x = PHOTOS_224["coffee"].clone().requires_grad_(True)   # (1, 3, 224, 224); we want the gradient w.r.t. x
logits = net(x)                                      # (1, 1000)
y_clean = logits.argmax(dim=1)                       # the class the network sees now
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y_clean)
loss.backward()                                      # x.grad: how the loss changes with each pixel
resnet.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)                   # we do not train: forget the weight gradients
probs_clean = F.softmax(logits.detach(), dim=1)[0]   # (1000,) probabilities
p_clean = probs_clean[y_clean].item()
print(f"clean photo: {categories[y_clean.item()]} ({100 * p_clean:.1f}%)")

fgsm = []                                            # one row per eps: (eps, class, probability, photo)
with torch.no_grad():
    for eps in EPS:
        # TODO: move every pixel by eps in the direction of the gradient: which function keeps only +1 or -1?
        x_adv = (x + ___ * x.grad.___()).clamp(0, 1)    # every pixel moves by +eps or -eps
        probs = F.softmax(net(x_adv), dim=1)[0]      # (1000,) probabilities for the changed photo
        top1, conf = probs.argmax().item(), probs.max().item()
        fgsm.append((eps, top1, conf, x_adv))
        print(f"ε = {eps:<6} top-1: {categories[top1]:22s} {100 * conf:5.1f}%")
Code What it means
class Normalized(nn.Module) A wrapper: pixels in [0, 1] go in, normalization happens inside, so eps is in real pixel units.
.clone().requires_grad_(True) A copy of the photo that PyTorch tracks: requires_grad asks for a gradient with respect to this tensor (the _ means “in place”).
loss.backward() After it, x.grad holds, for every pixel, how the loss changes with it.
x.grad.___() A tensor method that turns each number into -1, 0 or +1.

Hints ✏ (two blanks). The slide formula is x_adv = clip(x + ε · sign(∇ₓ loss), 0, 1). First blank: the step size: which variable does the for line give you? Second: the operation of the formula that keeps only the direction of the gradient (it is also a tensor method name). Expect: clean photo: espresso (93.4%), then one line per ε from 0.001 to 0.1: watch at which ε the class changes. The ✅ cell draws clean, noise and adversarial photos and prints the REPORT (smallest ε that changed the class, new class). Compare the three photos: can you see the change? (Lab 2, question Q2 asks whose weakness this is.) If you see: AttributeError: 'Tensor' object has no attribute '___' (method blank), TypeError ... 7 Lab 3 · Transfer learning

You reuse the 11 million weights of ResNet18 for CIFAR-10 with only 5,000 photos. Every pair does 3a (feature extraction) and 3b (fine-tuning).

7.1 L3·1 · the 5,000 photos and the number to beat (S2·L3·1)

What it does. Picks 5,000 training photos (500 per class) and 2,000 validation photos, defines prep, and trains the small warm-up ConvNet from scratch on the same photos: the number to beat. In: CIFAR-10 from S2·0. Out: tensors on the GPU, prep, one accuracy.

# S2·L3·1 (extract)
def prep(x):
    """A batch of 32 × 32 photos in [0, 1] -> IMG × IMG (224), normalized like ImageNet."""
    x = F.interpolate(x, size=(IMG, IMG), mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)   # (N, 3, 224, 224)
    return imagenet_norm(x)                     # the normalization ResNet18 was trained with

The baseline is trained with the helper fit(scratch, ...) of S2·0. prep(x) turns a batch (N, 3, 32, 32) into (N, 3, 224, 224) (resize, then ImageNet normalization), per batch, on the fly. The GPU keeps only the small 32 × 32 photos. The rest of the cell is plumbing: stratified picks the same number of photos from each class; SmallConvNet is the warm-up network written again, so that this lab works without the warm-up. Expect: train (5000, 3, 32, 32) · val (2000, 3, 32, 32), prep: (2, 3, 32, 32) -> (2, 3, 224, 224), ten epoch lines and a ✅ line. The baseline is about 49% (it takes about a second). Remember it.

7.2 L3·2 · the training loop for transfer learning (S2·L3·2)

What it does. Defines train_tl, used by 3a, 3b and the experiment. You write nothing here: read it, then run it. It is the same four steps as fit, plus prep on each batch and mixed precision (float16 maths on the GPU).

# S2·L3·2 (extract)
def amp():
    """Mixed precision (float16) on the GPU; nothing on a CPU."""
    if device == "cuda":
        return torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
# ...
    scaler = torch.amp.GradScaler("cuda") if device == "cuda" else None    # float16 needs a loss scaler
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    n, t0 = len(X3_train), time.time()
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # BatchNorm: train mode updates its running statistics, eval mode keeps the ImageNet ones
        model.eval() if freeze_bn else model.train()
        perm = torch.randperm(n, device=device)          # a new random order every epoch
        total = torch.zeros((), device=device)           # sum of the losses of this epoch
        for i in range(0, n, BATCH3):
            idx = perm[i:i + BATCH3]                     # the indices of one mini-batch of 64 photos
            with amp():
                loss = loss_fn(model(prep(X3_train[idx])), y3_train[idx])     # 1. forward, 2. loss
            optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
            if scaler is not None:                       # on the GPU: the scaler protects float16 gradients
                scaler.scale(loss).backward()                                  # 3. backward
                scaler.step(optimizer)                                         # 4. update
                scaler.update()
            else:                                        # on a CPU: the usual two lines
                loss.backward()                                                # 3. backward
                optimizer.step()                                               # 4. update
            total += loss.detach().float() * len(idx)
Code What it means
torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.float16) Inside with amp(): PyTorch uses 16-bit numbers where it is safe: about 2 times faster on a T4.
GradScaler Float16 has a small range, tiny gradients could become 0. The scaler multiplies the loss first and undoes it before the update.
model.eval() if freeze_bn else model.train() With freeze_bn=True the whole model stays in evaluation mode: BatchNorm keeps the ImageNet statistics (Lab 3a).
scaler.scale(loss).backward(), scaler.step(...), scaler.update() Steps 3 and 4 with the scaler.

Plumbing: evaluate_tl (validation accuracy in batches of 250), EPOCHS3, the final print. Expect: ready: 5,000 training photos, batches of 64, images 224 × 224, mixed precision on (on a CPU: off, and Lab 3 is very slow).

8 Lab 4 · Upsample, then segment the cat

Segmentation gives a class to every pixel: K × H × W scores for K classes. The encoder shrinks the maps; the decoder enlarges them with transpose convolutions.

8.1 TODO 1 · a transpose convolution (S2·L4·TODO1)

What it does. The opposite of a strided convolution: it enlarges the maps. Each input pixel paints a copy of the kernel; copies are added where they overlap. In: (1, 16, 7, 7). Out: (1, 8, 14, 14).

# ✏️ S2·L4·TODO1

try ... except catches a failed download and prints a message instead of stopping (not an error). seg_model(...)["out"]: this model returns a dictionary; the scores are under "out". out.argmax(dim=1)[0] picks, for every pixel, the class with the largest score. (mask == VOC.index("cat")).float().mean() is the fraction of “cat” pixels. Expect: two photos with colour masks; about three quarters of the cat photo is “cat” (the reference run is a little above 75%); the REPORT prints it. If you see Could not load the segmentation network (no internet?): skip the cell and look at the Lab 4 slide. The last cell, S2·END, prints all your REPORT lines and a table of all models.

9 Glossary

Word or function One line
logits, softmax Raw scores of the last layer; the function that turns them into probabilities adding to 1.
nn.Module Base class of a model: __init__ makes layers, forward runs them.
nn.Conv2d(C_in, C_out, M) Convolution with C_out filters of size M × M.
nn.MaxPool2d(2) Keeps the largest value of each 2 × 2 block.
.view, .flatten(1), .permute Change the shape or the order of the axes of a tensor.
.argmax(dim=1), .topk(k) Position of the largest value along an axis; the k largest values.
.item(), .detach(), .cpu() Tensor to Python number; cut from the gradient graph; move to the CPU.
.clamp(0, 1) Force values into a range.
requires_grad Switch on a parameter or tensor: compute its gradient or not.
state_dict(), load_state_dict() The dictionary of all parameters of a model, and loading it back.
register_forward_hook, register_hook Call your function when a layer runs (sees input and output); when a tensor’s gradient is computed.
torch.autocast, GradScaler Float16 maths where safe (faster); scales the loss so tiny float16 gradients survive.
Grad-CAM, FGSM Heat map of where a CNN looked; attack that moves each pixel by eps along the gradient direction.
backbone, head; feature extraction, fine-tuning The pretrained body and the last layers; train only a new head, or train everything with a small learning rate.
segmentation, REPORT line A class for every pixel (K × H × W scores); the numbers you say and type into Moodle.
